false_assumption.statement: Roger Gretorex was the murderer because he was the last to see Jervis alive and had access to arsenic.
false_assumption.why_it_seems_reasonable: Gretorex’s close relationship with Ivy and Jervis, his possession of arsenic, and his presence at the victim’s side made him the prime suspect. The prosecution’s narrative and the circumstantial evidence strongly pointed to him.
false_assumption.what_it_hides: It obscures Ivy Lexton’s secret access to the poison and her motive to kill her husband to gain freedom and wealth. It also hides the manipulation and falsehoods Ivy used to frame Gretorex.

mechanism_description: Ivy Lexton secretly obtained arsenic from Roger Gretorex’s surgery and administered it to her husband, Jervis Lexton, in his drinks and food over a period of time. She concealed her guilt by maintaining appearances and manipulating others, including providing false alibis and misleading witnesses. The evidence against Roger Gretorex was circumstantial and exploited by the prosecution, but new evidence from Mrs. Huntley and love letters revealed Ivy’s guilt, leading to a reprieve for Gretorex.

discriminating_test.design: Recreate the scene in Gretorex’s surgery where Mrs. Huntley saw Ivy alone with the arsenic jar. Mrs. Huntley identifies Ivy’s position and the presence of the poison. The test confirms Ivy’s opportunity to administer poison without witnesses.
discriminating_test.knowledge_revealed: Confirms Ivy’s access to arsenic and opportunity to poison her husband secretly.
discriminating_test.pass_condition: Witness testimony and physical layout prove Ivy was alone with arsenic at critical time.
